description: Wire vectors of the Fetch API (key 1, v0 to v11), replayed by tests/Compliance.

vectors.description: Fetch request v4, which adds the IsolationLevel byte behind the request-level MaxBytes of version 3 - 0, read_uncommitted. Its partition entries are the ones of version 3: the LogStartOffset only arrived in version 5.

The answer of that request: the record batch v2 as the log holds it, and the two fields version 4 added to a partition entry. A read_uncommitted fetch is answered with the LastStableOffset -1 and the element count -1 of a null AbortedTransactions array - the broker computes neither of them for a consumer that does not care about transactions.
Fetch request v5, which adds the LogStartOffset of a partition entry between its FetchOffset and its MaxBytes. Only a follower replica fills it in, an ordinary consumer sends -1.

The answer of that request. The LogStartOffset of the partition - 0, nothing has been deleted from the front of this log - stands between the LastStableOffset and the AbortedTransactions, and it is reported for a read_uncommitted fetch as well, unlike the other two.
The same request with the IsolationLevel 1, read_committed: the only byte of the frame that differs.

What read_committed changes about the answer of a partition that no transaction ever touched: the LastStableOffset is the real one - the high water mark, because everything below it is decided - and the AbortedTransactions array is present and empty, which is not the null of a read_uncommitted answer.

A read_committed answer of a partition whose only transaction was aborted: one entry in AbortedTransactions with the producer id of that transaction and the first offset it wrote. The record set still holds both batches - the transactional data batch at the offset 0 and the control batch with the ABORT marker that the coordinator wrote at the offset 1 - because the broker does not filter anything: dropping the records of an aborted producer is the job of the consumer.

Fetch request v2 of an ordinary consumer (ReplicaId = -1) for one partition, with a MaxBytes of 4096 for it. The frame is the one of version 1; the version alone tells the broker that the client understands message format v1, so the log is not converted down to format v0.

The answer of that request: the ThrottleTimeMs of version 1, the high water mark of the partition and the 97 bytes of the message set as the log holds them - two messages of format v1 (magic byte 1) with the CreateTime the producer stamped on them.
Fetch request v3, which adds the request-level MaxBytes after MinBytes: 8192 bytes for the whole answer, next to the 4096 bytes of the single partition.
The answer of the version 3 request is the answer of the version 2 one: the response frame did not change between v1, v2 and v3, only the correlation id of this capture differs.

Fetch request v3 for two partitions of one topic with a request-level MaxBytes of 40 bytes, which is less than a single message of either of them. The order of the partitions in this frame is the order in which the broker fills the answer.

What the broker answers to it: the first partition ignores the budget and returns its 52-byte message in full, so that the consumer can make progress, and the second one - whose turn comes when the 40 bytes are already used up - comes back with an empty message set although its high water mark shows that there is a message to read.
Fetch request v1 of an ordinary consumer (ReplicaId = -1) reading one partition from offset 0. The body is the one of v0, only the api version of the header differs.
Fetch response v1: the ThrottleTimeMs that version 1 put in front of the topics array (0, the broker enforces no consumer quota), then the high watermark and the message set of the partition.

Fetch response v1 of a client that exceeded its consumer_byte_rate quota: the fetch started at the high watermark and returned no records at all, and the broker still delayed the answer by 5943 ms because the byte rate of the window was over the quota.
Fetch request v0 of an ordinary consumer (ReplicaId = -1) reading one partition from offset 0.
Fetch response v0 with the high watermark and the message set that the produce vector wrote, and without the ThrottleTimeMs prefix that v1 added.

Fetch v5 answer of a `read_committed` consumer of a partition that holds one **aborted** transaction: the last stable offset is 3, past everything, and `aborted_transactions` names the producer id 2 with the first offset 0. The answer nevertheless carries both aborted records and the ABORT control batch - a 0.11.0.3 broker does not filter them out, it names them and leaves the filtering to the client.
Fetch v6 of one partition. The frame is the one of version 5, byte for byte; what the version states is that the client understands the error code 56 KAFKA_STORAGE_ERROR.
The answer of that request: the version 5 frame, without the top-level error code and session id that version 7 inserted behind the throttle time.

Fetch v7 with the epoch 0 and the session id 0, i.e. a full fetch that asks the broker to open an incremental fetch session (KIP-227). The two int32 sit between the isolation level and the topics; the empty array behind the topics is the forgotten_topics_data.

The answer of that request. The top-level error code 0 and the session id the broker handed out stand between the throttle time and the topics; a full fetch is answered with every partition it asked for.
The incremental fetch that follows: the same session id with the next epoch and an EMPTY topics array, which says "the partitions of the session, with the fetch parameters you already know".
The answer of that incremental fetch: only the partition whose log grew since the previous answer. The other partition of the session is silently left out.
An incremental fetch that drops a partition from its session: the partition travels in the forgotten_topics_data array behind the topics, and the broker stops answering for it.
The answer of that request: the partition had a record appended to it right before the fetch, and it is still left out - it is gone from the session, and therefore from every answer of it.

The answer to an incremental fetch whose epoch is not the one the broker expects: the error code 71 INVALID_FETCH_SESSION_EPOCH, the session id 0 and an EMPTY topics array. The session itself survives.
The answer to an incremental fetch whose session id the broker does not know: the error code 70 FETCH_SESSION_ID_NOT_FOUND, the session id 0 and an EMPTY topics array.

The incremental fetch of a consumer whose assignment changed: the topics array carries the positions that moved since the last request - and only those - while the partition that left the assignment travels in forgotten_topics_data. This is what FetchSessionHandler builds after a rebalance.
The answer of that request: the forgotten partition is gone from the session, and of the two that are left only the one whose log grew is answered.

The way back from the error codes 70 and 71: the session id the client holds with the epoch 0, which is a full fetch - it removes the session the broker may still have and asks for a new one in the same request, FetchMetadata::nextCloseExisting().
The answer of that full fetch: a NEW session id - the broker never reuses the old one - and every partition the request asked for.

Fetch request v8 of one partition from the offset 0, session-less (session id 0, epoch -1) and with an empty forgotten_topics_data array. The body is the body of version 7, byte for byte - FetchRequest.json @ 2.8.2 says "Version 8 is the same as version 7" - and what version 8 (Kafka 2.0, KIP-219) states is that the client waits out the throttle time of the answer itself.

Fetch response v8 of the partition the request above produced to: the throttle time, the top-level error code and the session id 0 of a session-less fetch, then the partition with its high water mark, its last stable offset, its log start offset, the null aborted-transactions array of a read_uncommitted fetch and the record batch of the message format v2 as it lies in the log.

The answer of a Fetch v8 request that a consumer_byte_rate quota of 1024 bytes per second throttled: the throttle_time_ms of 70 ms at the head of the frame, the top-level error code 0, the session id 0 of a session-less fetch and an EMPTY topics array - a throttled fetch is answered with no partition at all, so there is nothing for the consumer to read and nothing but the throttle time to act on. The answer arrived about 1 ms after the request was written.

Fetch request v3 of a partition whose topic is configured with message.downconversion.enable = false. A version 3 request can only read the message formats v0 and v1, so the broker would have to convert the record batch v2 of the log down for it.

The answer of a 2.8.2 broker to the request above: the error code 43 UNSUPPORTED_VERSION for the partition, with an empty record set, instead of the converted batch a broker below KIP-283 (Kafka 2.0) would have built. The high water mark travels as -1 next to the error.

Fetch request v9 of one partition from the offset 0 with the current_leader_epoch 0, the epoch of a partition that has been led by the same broker since it was created. The field sits between the partition index and the fetch offset - the field order of FetchRequest.json @ 2.8.2, which is the wire order.
The answer of that request: the frame of version 7, byte for byte - FetchResponse.json @ 2.8.2 has no field between version 7 and version 11 - with the records of the partition.
The same Fetch v9 with the current_leader_epoch 1, one above the epoch the partition is really led with: a belief from the future, which the leader refuses.

The answer of the request above: the error code 75 UNKNOWN_LEADER_EPOCH for the partition, with the high water mark -1 and an empty record set. 74 FENCED_LEADER_EPOCH is the other direction - an epoch BELOW the current one - and a one-broker container never re-elects a leader, so it can not be produced here.

Fetch request v10 of one partition from the offset 0 with the current_leader_epoch 0. The body is the body of version 9, byte for byte - FetchRequest.json @ 2.8.2 has no field of version 10 - and what version 10 (Kafka 2.1, KIP-110) states is that the client understands a zstd-compressed record batch. This is the version this client sends.
The answer of that request: the frame of version 7, byte for byte, with the records of the partition.
A Fetch v9 of a topic configured with compression.type=zstd. Version 9 is the last one that does not promise to understand the codec of KIP-110.

The answer of a 2.8.2 broker: the error code 76 UNSUPPORTED_COMPRESSION_TYPE for the partition, with the high water mark -1 and an empty record set. KafkaApis.handleFetchRequest @ 2.8.2 refuses every fetch below version 10 of a partition whose TOPIC is configured with compression.type = zstd, whatever the records really are.

The same partition fetched with version 10, which promises the codec: the broker answers the record batch as it lies, with the compression type 4 in its attributes. Reading the records out of it needs ext-zstd; without the extension this client throws an UnsupportedCompressionTypeException, the client-side half of the code 76.

Fetch request v11 (Kafka 2.3, KIP-392) with a rack_id: the field is the LAST one of the frame, behind the forgotten_topics_data of KIP-227 - the field order of FetchRequest.json @ 2.8.2. The leader of the partition reads it to pick the replica this consumer should read from.

The answer of that request: every partition entry carries a preferred_read_replica between its aborted transactions and its record set. It is -1 here, "read from me": the container runs without a replica.selector.class, so its leader never hands a reader to a follower, whatever rack the request names.
